title: Cheap and Accurate Enough: Sampling
subtitle: Spend retention on signal and preserve sampling weights
summary: Pip reduces telemetry volume and loses a rare customer failure. Sampling preserves complete retained events, not every event. Head, tail, and adaptive choices see different information; known retention probabilities support honest estimates without recreating discarded details.

concepts.title: Constant probability preserves examples
concepts.body: Pip retains each event with a constant 1% probability. Frequent behavior may remain representative, but one unusual failure is very likely absent. Sampling preserves the full recorded context of retained requests unlike aggregation. Pip cannot promise that a particular customer’s event survived or that every small cohort has an example.

concepts.title: Head and tail know different facts
concepts.body: Pip wants to keep error traces after their outcome is known. Head sampling decides near entry, before final status or duration; tail sampling waits for that information. Errors and slow traces can then receive preference. Pip budgets pending-span handling and coordinated retention because the extra knowledge has operational costs.

concepts.title: Dynamic rates protect useful cohorts
concepts.body: Pip’s busiest stall overwhelms quieter tenants in the global sample. Dynamic rates can adapt to recent volume and sampling keys such as tenant and outcome. Rare cohorts need deliberate retention, while keeping every error can fail during an error surge. Pip designs rates around both useful evidence and the telemetry budget.

concepts.title: Weights enable honest estimates
concepts.body: Pip keeps successes at 1% and errors at 100%. Their inverse-probability weights are 100 and 1, so unequal retention requires weighted counts and distributions. Known nonzero probability supports estimates, not naïve averages over rows. Pip cannot restore discarded detail, remove variance, or infer populations given zero retention probability.

misconceptions.claim: Keeping every error means the retained error percentage equals the service error rate.
misconceptions.correction: If successes are sampled more heavily, use the recorded probabilities to weight both populations.

misconceptions.claim: Dynamic sampling guarantees every rare failure is captured.
misconceptions.correction: It can improve representation, but retention policy, volume, and chance still limit which examples survive.

scenario.title: The sampled error rate looks enormous
scenario.context: Every error is retained while only 1% of successes survive; the raw stored rows look mostly unhealthy.

options.label: Apply recorded inverse-probability weights
options.benefit: Produces an estimate that accounts for unequal retention.
options.cost: Still has sampling uncertainty and cannot recreate missing examples.
options.consequence: The estimated service rate differs from the intentionally error-heavy composition of stored rows.

options.label: Report the unweighted retained-row percentage
options.benefit: Describes the composition of the stored sample.
options.cost: Misrepresents the service population under unequal selection.
options.consequence: Stakeholders may infer a severe production failure from a deliberately biased sample.

scenario.debrief: Name whether a result describes retained data or estimates original traffic, and preserve probabilities needed for the latter.

quiz.question: A retained success has probability 0.01 and a retained error probability 1. Which weights apply?
quiz.explanation: Inverse-probability weighting reflects how many original events each retained row represents.

quiz.question: Which approach can use final request latency to make its selection?
options: A constant decision independent of the outcome
Tail sampling after outcome information arrives
quiz.explanation: Tail selection gains outcome knowledge at the cost of buffering and coordination.

quiz.question: Why sample by tenant as well as total traffic volume?
options: To improve representation of quiet tenants that global sampling may miss
To use the same retention probability without considering each tenant’s volume
To calculate population rates from unweighted retained-row counts
quiz.explanation: Per-key policies can protect rare cohorts, while weights and uncertainty still matter.

exercise.title: Design a sampling policy
exercise.prompt: Specify how to preserve a rare customer cohort while keeping telemetry volume manageable.
